claim: Area TE is located in the inferior temporal cortex and is part of the ventral visual stream.
source: A half-century of behavioral, anatomical and physiological research has revealed that this feat of visual perception is supported by a sequence of connected brain regions stretching from the occipital cortex to inferior temporal cortex (Figure 1A) (Gross et al., 1972; Ungerleider and Mishkin, 1982).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research and reference to Figure 1A showing anatomical location

claim: Simple features such as oriented edges or lines are represented in area V1.
source: Simple features, such as oriented edges or lines, are represented in caudal regions, beginning with area V1 (Hubel and Wiesel, 1959).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hubel and Wiesel, 1959

claim: Conjunctions of features defining whole objects are represented in area TE.
source: Conjunctions of features defining whole objects are represented in rostral regions, culminating with area TE (Kobatake and Tanaka, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kobatake and Tanaka, 1994

claim: Rhinal cortex is directly adjacent to area TE.
source: Directly adjacent to area TE is rhinal cortex, an anatomically distinct region that receives dense projections from area TE (Suzuki and Amaral, 1994), and is thought to be important primarily for memory function (Meunier et al., 1993; Higuchi and Miyashita, 1996).
evidence: Stated in text and supported by anatomical citations

claim: Rhinal cortex receives dense projections from area TE.
source: Directly adjacent to area TE is rhinal cortex, an anatomically distinct region that receives dense projections from area TE (Suzuki and Amaral, 1994), and is thought to be important primarily for memory function (Meunier et al., 1993; Higuchi and Miyashita, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Suzuki and Amaral, 1994

claim: Rhinal cortex is thought to be important primarily for memory function.
source: Directly adjacent to area TE is rhinal cortex, an anatomically distinct region that receives dense projections from area TE (Suzuki and Amaral, 1994), and is thought to be important primarily for memory function (Meunier et al., 1993; Higuchi and Miyashita, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Meunier et al., 1993 and Higuchi and Miyashita, 1996

claim: It has been suggested that rhinal cortex is important for visual perception of complex objects or objects with overlapping features.
source: It has more recently been suggested that rhinal cortex is important for visual perception of complex objects or objects with over-lapping features, and hence might be considered the final stage of the visual perceptual processing hierarchy (Buckley et al., 2001; Bussey et al., 2003; Baxter, 2009), but see Hampton, 2005, Suzuki (2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buckley et al., 2001; Bussey et al., 2003; Baxter, 2009, with contrasting views from Hampton, 2005 and Suzuki, 2009

claim: Three groups of three monkeys were tested: an unoperated control group, a group with bilateral removal of area TE, and a group with bilateral removal of rhinal cortex.
source: We tested three groups of three monkeys: an unoperated control group, a group with a bilateral removal of area TE, and a group with a bilateral removal of rhinal cortex (including peri- and ento- rhinal cortex).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section

claim: Monkeys were trained to perform a cat vs. dog category discrimination in a visually cued two-interval forced choice (2-IFC) paradigm.
source: Monkeys were trained to perform a cat vs. dog category discrimination in a visually cued two-interval forced choice (2-IFC) paradigm (Figure 1B) (Matsumoto et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated in text with reference to Figure 1B and citation to Matsumoto et al., 2016

claim: Monkeys responded while a stimulus was present, thereby minimizing demands on short-term memory.
source: The monkeys responded while a stimulus was present, thereby minimizing demands on short-term memory.
evidence: Directly stated as a design feature of the task

claim: In Experiment 1, monkeys were presented with stimuli comprising cats, dogs, and intermediate morphed images spaced at 10% increments from 0% to 100% dog.
source: In Experiment 1, monkeys were presented with a set of stimuli comprising cats, dogs, and intermediate morphed images spaced at 10% increments on an arbitrary scale (Abrosoft, Beijing, China) from 0 % to 100% dog (Figure 1C).
evidence: Stated in text with reference to Figure 1C showing example stimuli

claim: Monkeys in all three groups classified most stimuli well the first time they were presented in Experiment 1.
source: The monkeys in all three groups classified most stimuli well the first time they were presented (Figure 2A,B,C).
evidence: Stated in text with reference to Figure 2A, B, C showing performance data

claim: The control and rhinal-removal groups improved quickly with repetition, reaching asymptotic performance by the 10th repeat of the stimulus set in Experiment 1.
source: The control and rhinal-removal groups improved quickly with repetition, reaching asymptotic performance by the 10th repeat of the stimulus set (Figure 2D).
evidence: Stated in text with reference to Figure 2D showing learning curves

claim: The TE-removal group was slower to learn in Experiment 1, only reaching the level of performance of controls by the 14th repetition of the stimulus set.
source: The TE-removal group was slower to learn, only reaching the level of performance of controls by the 14th repetition of the stimulus set.
evidence: Stated in text describing results from Experiment 1

claim: Across presentations in Experiment 1, the group with TE removals categorized less accurately than the control group (LME, p=0.0072, z = 2.69).
source: Across presentations, the group with TE removals categorized less accurately than the control group (Linear Mixed Effects model, LME, p=0.0072, z = 2.69).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Linear Mixed Effects model) with reported p-value and z-score

claim: There was an interaction effect between number of presentations by treatment group (Ctl vs. TE) by morph level in Experiment 1 (LME, p=1.07×10−8, z = −5.72).
source: The deficit seen in the TE-removal group might be attributable to slower learning, as there was an interaction effect between number of presentations by treatment group (Ctl vs. TE) by morph level (LME, p=1.07×10−8, z = −5.72).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis with reported p-value and z-score

claim: The performance of the group with rhinal removals was indistinguishable from that of controls in Experiment 1 (LME, p=0.23, z = −1.19).
source: The performance of the group with rhinal removals was indistinguishable from that of controls (LME, p=0.23, z = −1.19).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference

claim: In Experiment 2, stimuli consisted of the following ratios of cat:dog: 100:0, 75:25, 65:35, 60:40, 55:45, 50:50, 45:55, 40:60, 35:65, 25:75, and 0:100.
source: We continued to explore the full range of category space (from 0% to 100% dog), but biased the distribution of stimuli towards the category boundary (cat 50:50 dog) by presenting stimuli consisting of the following ratios of cat:dog: 100:0, 75:25, 65:35, 60:40, 55:45, 50:50, 45:55, 40:60, 35:65, 25:75, and 0:100 (supplementary Figure 1).
evidence: Stated in text with reference to supplementary Figure 1

claim: The asymmetrical reward structure of the task design produced a bias in all treatment groups toward classifying ambiguous stimuli as dogs.
source: The asymmetrical reward structure of the task design produced a bias in all treatment groups toward classifying ambiguous stimuli as dogs, that is at the 50% morph level an unbiased subject would report the stimuli as dog-like 50% of the time.
evidence: Stated as an observation about the effect of task design on behavior

claim: Control monkeys reported the 50:50 morphs as more dog-like on 70% of presentations in Experiment 2.
source: However, control monkeys reported the 50:50 morphs as more dog-like on 70% of presentations.
evidence: Stated as a specific data point from Experiment 2

claim: The rhinal-lesioned group showed a similar bias, reporting 64% as more dog-like for 50:50 morphs in Experiment 2.
source: The rhinal-lesioned group showed a similar bias, reporting 64% as more dog-like.
evidence: Stated as a specific data point from Experiment 2

claim: The TE-lesioned group showed a bias in the same direction as the other two groups, reporting 50:50 morphs as more dog-like 61% of the time in Experiment 2.
source: The TE-lesioned group showed a bias in the same direction as the other two groups, reporting 50:50 morphs as more dog-like 61% of the time.
evidence: Stated as a specific data point from Experiment 2

claim: All groups had reached asymptotic performance by the tenth presentation of the stimuli in Experiment 2.
source: For Experiment 2, all groups had reached asymptotic performance by the tenth presentation of the stimuli.
evidence: Stated as an observation about learning in Experiment 2

claim: During presentations 11 to 20 of Experiment 2, the categorization accuracy of monkeys with bilateral aspiration removals of rhinal cortex was indistinguishable from that of controls (LME, p=0.49, z = −0.68).
source: During presentations 11 to 20, the categorization accuracy of monkeys with bilateral aspiration removals of rhinal cortex was indistinguishable from that of controls (LME, p=0.49, z = −0.68).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference

claim: Monkeys with bilateral TE removals made significantly more incorrect assignments than the other two groups during presentations 11 to 20 of Experiment 2 (LME, p=2.64×10−10, z = −6.32).
source: Monkeys with bilateral TE removals made significantly more incorrect assignments than the other two groups (LME, p=2.64×10−10, z = −6.32), but nonetheless categorized better than would be expected by chance (t test, p=0.00057, d.f. = 5, t = −7.49) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis with reported p-values and reference to Figure 3A

claim: Monkeys with bilateral TE removals categorized better than would be expected by chance in Experiment 2 (t test, p=0.00057, d.f. = 5, t = −7.49).
source: Monkeys with bilateral TE removals made significantly more incorrect assignments than the other two groups (LME, p=2.64×10−10, z = −6.32), but nonetheless categorized better than would be expected by chance (t test, p=0.00057, d.f. = 5, t = −7.49) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by t-test statistical analysis with reported p-value

claim: Performance of all three test groups was stable throughout the latter 10 presentations of the test stimuli in Experiment 2 (LME, effect of repetition, p=0.54, z = −0.61).
source: It seems unlikely that the impairment in making visual category discriminations following TE removals could be attributed to a learning deficit, because performance of all three test groups was stable throughout the latter 10 presentations of the test stimuli (LME, effect of repetition, p=0.54, z = −0.61).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing no effect of repetition

claim: For all monkeys, the closer the stimulus was to the category boundary, the longer it took to release the lever on correct trials during the presence of the red target (LME – effect of morph level, p=0.0017, d.f. = 5, t = 5.23).
source: For all monkeys, the closer the stimulus was to the category boundary, the longer it took to release the lever on correct trials during the presence of the red target (LME – effect of morph level, p=0.0017, d.f. = 5, t = 5.23) (Figure 3B,C,D), supporting the inference that classification is more difficult near the category boundary.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 3B, C, D showing reaction time data

claim: Classification is more difficult near the category boundary.
source: For all monkeys, the closer the stimulus was to the category boundary, the longer it took to release the lever on correct trials during the presence of the red target (LME – effect of morph level, p=0.0017, d.f. = 5, t = 5.23) (Figure 3B,C,D), supporting the inference that classification is more difficult near the category boundary.
evidence: Inferred from reaction time data showing longer latencies near the boundary

claim: The latency to release following the green target was constant across difficulty levels because the monkeys had presumably made the decision that the stimulus was dog-like earlier in the trial (LME – effect of morph level, p=0.40, d.f. = 5, t = 0.26).
source: The latency to release following the green target was constant across difficulty levels because the monkeys had presumably made the decision that the stimulus was dog-like earlier in the trial (LME – effect of morph level, p=0.40, d.f. = 5, t = 0.26).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing no effect of morph level, with inference about decision timing

claim: Reaction times did not differ across groups in Experiment 2.
source: Reaction times did not differ across groups, suggesting that TE removal did not slow the decision process (reaction times during red target (LME, p=0.15, d.f. = 2, t = 1.35)), nor did it slow the basic visual-motor reaction time (reaction time during green target (LME, p=0.48, d.f. = 2, t = −0.069)).
evidence: Supported by statistical analyses showing no significant differences in reaction times

claim: TE removal did not slow the decision process.
source: Reaction times did not differ across groups, suggesting that TE removal did not slow the decision process (reaction times during red target (LME, p=0.15, d.f. = 2, t = 1.35)), nor did it slow the basic visual-motor reaction time (reaction time during green target (LME, p=0.48, d.f. = 2, t = −0.069)).
evidence: Inferred from lack of difference in reaction times during red target presentation

claim: TE removal did not slow the basic visual-motor reaction time.
source: Reaction times did not differ across groups, suggesting that TE removal did not slow the decision process (reaction times during red target (LME, p=0.15, d.f. = 2, t = 1.35)), nor did it slow the basic visual-motor reaction time (reaction time during green target (LME, p=0.48, d.f. = 2, t = −0.069)).
evidence: Inferred from lack of difference in reaction times during green target presentation

claim: Grating contrast-sensitivity was indistinguishable across all three groups (Ctl vs TE: LME, p=0.28, d.f. = 2, t = −0.69; Ctl vs Rh: LME, p=0.22, d.f. = 2, t = −0.95).
source: The deficits observed in the TE group are also unlikely to be due to a failure in basic visual acuity, because grating contrast-sensitivity – a test designed to assess the visual acuity of human subjects (Blakemore and Campbell, 1969) - was indistinguishable across all three groups (Ctl vs TE: LME, p=0.28, d.f. = 2, t = −0.69; Ctl vs Rh: LME, p=0.22, d.f. = 2, t = −0.95)) (Figure 4), and similar to those of humans (Blakemore and Campbell, 1969).
evidence: Supported by statistical analyses and reference to Figure 4 showing contrast sensitivity data

claim: The contrast sensitivity of the monkeys was similar to those of humans.
source: The deficits observed in the TE group are also unlikely to be due to a failure in basic visual acuity, because grating contrast-sensitivity – a test designed to assess the visual acuity of human subjects (Blakemore and Campbell, 1969) - was indistinguishable across all three groups (Ctl vs TE: LME, p=0.28, d.f. = 2, t = −0.69; Ctl vs Rh: LME, p=0.22, d.f. = 2, t = −0.95)) (Figure 4), and similar to those of humans (Blakemore and Campbell, 1969).
evidence: Stated in text with citation to Blakemore and Campbell, 1969, and reference to Figure 4

claim: The deficits observed in the TE group are unlikely to be due to a failure in basic visual acuity.
source: The deficits observed in the TE group are also unlikely to be due to a failure in basic visual acuity, because grating contrast-sensitivity – a test designed to assess the visual acuity of human subjects (Blakemore and Campbell, 1969) - was indistinguishable across all three groups (Ctl vs TE: LME, p=0.28, d.f. = 2, t = −0.69; Ctl vs Rh: LME, p=0.22, d.f. = 2, t = −0.95)) (Figure 4), and similar to those of humans (Blakemore and Campbell, 1969).
evidence: Inferred from normal contrast sensitivity in TE-lesioned monkeys

claim: There were few late bar release errors (<1% on average) across all groups.
source: Motivation and attention did not seem to be altered in either lesion group because the reaction times of all groups were indistinguishable, and there were few late bar release errors (<1% on average) – the few late release errors that were recorded were not distributed significantly differently among the treatment groups (Kruskal-Wallis, χ2 = 2.49, p=0.29).
evidence: Stated as a data point about error rates

claim: Late release errors were not distributed significantly differently among the treatment groups (Kruskal-Wallis, χ2 = 2.49, p=0.29).
source: Motivation and attention did not seem to be altered in either lesion group because the reaction times of all groups were indistinguishable, and there were few late bar release errors (<1% on average) – the few late release errors that were recorded were not distributed significantly differently among the treatment groups (Kruskal-Wallis, χ2 = 2.49, p=0.29).
evidence: Supported by Kruskal-Wallis statistical test

claim: Motivation and attention did not seem to be altered in either lesion group.
source: Motivation and attention did not seem to be altered in either lesion group because the reaction times of all groups were indistinguishable, and there were few late bar release errors (<1% on average) – the few late release errors that were recorded were not distributed significantly differently among the treatment groups (Kruskal-Wallis, χ2 = 2.49, p=0.29).
evidence: Inferred from similar reaction times and error rates across groups

claim: Experiment 3 tested the possibility that monkeys with large cortical removals had compensated for a deficit in object perception/categorization by memorizing one or more simple diagnostic features of each morph series.
source: Experiment 3 tested the possibility that monkeys with large cortical removals (TE/rhinal) had compensated for a deficit in object perception/categorization by memorizing one or more simple diagnostic features of each morph series (e.g. the 'tail' of the stimuli in the second row of Figure 1C).
evidence: Stated as the rationale for Experiment 3

claim: Monkeys with perirhinal cortex lesions have been shown to perform indistinguishably from controls in discriminating perceptually dissimilar stimuli obscured by masks.
source: It has been demonstrated previously that the performance of monkeys with perirhinal cortex lesions is indistinguishable from controls in discriminating perceptually dissimilar stimuli obscured by masks (Hampton and Murray, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hampton and Murray, 2002

claim: Monkeys with bilateral TE removals were severely impaired by the masks relative to their own overall performance in the inter-leaved unmasked trials in Experiment 3 (LME, p=2×10−16, z = 9.03).
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, monkeys with bilateral TE removals were severely impaired by the masks relative to their own overall performance in the inter-leaved unmasked trials (Figure 5D) (LME, p=2×10−16, z = 9.03).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 5D

claim: Monkeys with bilateral TE removals categorized the masked stimuli significantly less accurately than controls in Experiment 3 (LME, p=0.0017, z = 3.13).
source: They categorized the masked stimuli significantly less accurately than controls (Figure 5B) (LME, p=0.0017, z = 3.13).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 5B

claim: The performance of controls and that of monkeys with rhinal removals was indistinguishable in Experiment 3 (LME, p=0.20, z = −1.27).
source: The performance of controls and that of monkeys with rhinal removals was indistinguishable (LME, p=0.20, z = −1.27); both groups exhibited smaller reductions in classification accuracy than the TE group in the presence of the masks, relative to the inter-leaved unmasked trials (Figure 5C,E) (Ctl: LME, p=8.92×10−11, z = 6.48; rhinal: LME, p=1.33×10−10, z = 6.42).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 5C, E

claim: Both control and rhinal-lesioned groups exhibited smaller reductions in classification accuracy than the TE group in the presence of the masks in Experiment 3 (Ctl: LME, p=8.92×10−11, z = 6.48; rhinal: LME, p=1.33×10−10, z = 6.42).
source: The performance of controls and that of monkeys with rhinal removals was indistinguishable (LME, p=0.20, z = −1.27); both groups exhibited smaller reductions in classification accuracy than the TE group in the presence of the masks, relative to the inter-leaved unmasked trials (Figure 5C,E) (Ctl: LME, p=8.92×10−11, z = 6.48; rhinal: LME, p=1.33×10−10, z = 6.42).
evidence: Supported by statistical analyses and reference to Figure 5C, E

claim: When monkeys fail to discriminate between the two offers due to the asymmetrical reward structure, they will usually resort to releasing the lever during the presence of the green target 100% of the time.
source: Due to the asymmetrical reward structure of this and similar tasks, when monkeys fail to discriminate between the two offers they will usually resort to releasing the lever during the presence of the green target 100% of the time, as this is the only condition in which reward is available.
evidence: Stated as an explanation for behavioral strategy under task constraints

claim: In Experiment 4, a large set of novel morphs were used as trial-unique stimuli in a single session.
source: In Experiment 4, a large set of novel morphs were used as trial-unique stimuli in a single session to control for the possibility that the monkeys memorized individual stimulus-response outcomes in Experiments 1, 2 and 3.
evidence: Stated as the design of Experiment 4

claim: Visual discrimination of complex stimuli can be performed independently of area TE and of rhinal cortex if the stimuli have become sufficiently well learned.
source: It has been demonstrated that visual discrimination of complex stimuli can be performed independently of area TE and of rhinal cortex if the stimuli have become sufficiently well learned (Eacott et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eacott et al., 1994

claim: In Experiment 4, each cat was morphed with two dogs, and vice versa.
source: We morphed a set of cat images each with two dog images, and vice versa (Figure 6A, supplementary Figure 2).
evidence: Stated in text with reference to Figure 6A and supplementary Figure 2

claim: Monkeys lacking area TE categorized stimuli significantly less accurately than controls in Experiment 4 (LME, p=2×10−16, z = 9.18).
source: Consistent with the results of Experiment 3, monkeys lacking area TE categorized stimuli significantly less accurately than controls (LME, p=2×10−16, z = 9.18), whereas those with rhinal cortex removals were indistinguishable from controls (Figure 6B) (LME, p=−0.62, z = −0.50).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 6B

claim: Monkeys with rhinal cortex removals were indistinguishable from controls in Experiment 4 (LME, p=−0.62, z = −0.50).
source: Consistent with the results of Experiment 3, monkeys lacking area TE categorized stimuli significantly less accurately than controls (LME, p=2×10−16, z = 9.18), whereas those with rhinal cortex removals were indistinguishable from controls (Figure 6B) (LME, p=−0.62, z = −0.50).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 6B

claim: Area TE is only important for perceiving and classifying objects with complex overlapping features, especially when novel/unfamiliar.
source: The results from the experiments described above suggest that area TE is only important for perceiving and classifying objects with complex over-lapping features, especially when novel/unfamiliar.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the experimental results

claim: The monkeys with TE removals were surprisingly good at classifying all but the most ambiguous stimuli.
source: The monkeys with TE removals were surprisingly good at classifying all but the most ambiguous stimuli (i.e. those closest to the category boundary).
evidence: Stated as an observation from the experimental results

claim: Perception of simple, low-level features appears to be intact in the monkeys lacking TE.
source: Perception of simple, low-level features appears to be intact in the monkeys lacking TE as shown by their normal ability to detect the change in color of the target from red to green in Experiments 1 – 4, and by their normal contrast sensitivity when tested with black and white sine wave gratings.
evidence: Inferred from normal performance on color detection and contrast sensitivity tasks

claim: Previous reports of deficits in visually guided behavior following rhinal removals may be attributable to memory deficits.
source: The lack of evidence for a role of rhinal cortex in perceptual processing reported here suggests that previous reports of deficits in visually guided behavior following rhinal removals may be attributable to memory deficits.
evidence: Inferred from the current results showing no perceptual deficit in rhinal-lesioned monkeys

claim: Monkeys lacking rhinal cortex are impaired in object recognition.
source: In behavioral testing, monkeys lacking rhinal cortex are impaired in object recognition (Meunier et al., 1993), and learning stimulus-stimulus associations (Murray et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Meunier et al., 1993 and Murray et al., 1993

claim: Monkeys lacking rhinal cortex are impaired in learning stimulus-stimulus associations.
source: In behavioral testing, monkeys lacking rhinal cortex are impaired in object recognition (Meunier et al., 1993), and learning stimulus-stimulus associations (Murray et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to Murray et al., 1993

claim: Monkeys lacking rhinal cortex are severely impaired in comparing reward values across time.
source: They are also severely impaired in comparing reward values across time (Liu et al., 2000), even when vision plays no role in the task (Clark et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liu et al., 2000 and Clark et al., 2012

claim: Rhinal cortex neurons appear to be tuned for complex stimuli in a similar manner to those recorded in area TE.
source: Rhinal cortex neurons appear to be tuned for complex stimuli in a similar manner to those recorded in area TE.
evidence: Stated as a general observation about neuronal properties

claim: Neuronal responses in TE generally exhibit task-invariant tuning for specific stimuli.
source: However, neuronal responses in TE generally exhibit task-invariant tuning for specific stimuli (McMahon et al., 2014), whereas neuronal responses in rhinal cortex are modulated by behavioral context (Yakovlev et al., 1998; Lehky and Tanaka, 2007; Naya and Suzuki, 2011; Eradath et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to McMahon et al., 2014

claim: Neuronal responses in rhinal cortex are modulated by behavioral context.
source: However, neuronal responses in TE generally exhibit task-invariant tuning for specific stimuli (McMahon et al., 2014), whereas neuronal responses in rhinal cortex are modulated by behavioral context (Yakovlev et al., 1998; Lehky and Tanaka, 2007; Naya and Suzuki, 2011; Eradath et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yakovlev et al., 1998; Lehky and Tanaka, 2007; Naya and Suzuki, 2011; Eradath et al., 2015

claim: When the stimulus-mapping in a delay-discounting task is randomized, perirhinal neurons lose their selectivity on the next trial.
source: For example, when the stimulus-mapping in a delay-discounting task is randomized, perirhinal neurons lose their selectivity on the next trial (Liu and Richmond, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu and Richmond, 2000

claim: The loss of stimulus selectivity in perirhinal neurons following a contextual change implies that the apparent selectivity is derived from a learned association with predicted outcome.
source: The loss of stimulus selectivity in perirhinal neurons following a contextual change implies that the apparent selectivity is derived from a learned association with predicted outcome.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that selectivity is lost when context changes

claim: Rhinal cortex neurons are sensitive to learned stimulus-stimulus associations.
source: Rhinal cortex neurons are also sensitive to learned stimulus-stimulus associations; they form a functional microcircuit that is dynamically modulated by task demand (Erickson and Desimone, 1999; Hirabayashi et al., 2013) and they convey information relevant to behavioral choice in a more accessible manner than those in TE (Pagan et al., 2013; Pagan and Rust, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Erickson and Desimone, 1999; Hirabayashi et al., 2013

claim: Rhinal cortex neurons form a functional microcircuit that is dynamically modulated by task demand.
source: Rhinal cortex neurons are also sensitive to learned stimulus-stimulus associations; they form a functional microcircuit that is dynamically modulated by task demand (Erickson and Desimone, 1999; Hirabayashi et al., 2013) and they convey information relevant to behavioral choice in a more accessible manner than those in TE (Pagan et al., 2013; Pagan and Rust, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Erickson and Desimone, 1999; Hirabayashi et al., 2013

claim: Rhinal cortex neurons convey information relevant to behavioral choice in a more accessible manner than those in TE.
source: Rhinal cortex neurons are also sensitive to learned stimulus-stimulus associations; they form a functional microcircuit that is dynamically modulated by task demand (Erickson and Desimone, 1999; Hirabayashi et al., 2013) and they convey information relevant to behavioral choice in a more accessible manner than those in TE (Pagan et al., 2013; Pagan and Rust, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pagan et al., 2013; Pagan and Rust, 2014

claim: The delay between TE and perirhinal neural responses to visual stimuli is considerably longer (~60 ms) than is usually attributed to a direct feed-forward mechanism (10–15 ms).
source: Furthermore, the delay between TE and perirhinal neural responses to visual stimuli is considerably longer (~60 ms) than is usually attributed to a direct feed-forward mechanism (10–15 ms) (Xiang and Brown, 1998; Liu and Richmond, 2000); this suggests that rhinal cortex is doing more than a simple monosynaptic transformation of visual input from TE neurons.
evidence: Supported by citations to Xiang and Brown, 1998; Liu and Richmond, 2000

claim: The long delay between TE and perirhinal neural responses suggests that rhinal cortex is doing more than a simple monosynaptic transformation of visual input from TE neurons.
source: Furthermore, the delay between TE and perirhinal neural responses to visual stimuli is considerably longer (~60 ms) than is usually attributed to a direct feed-forward mechanism (10–15 ms) (Xiang and Brown, 1998; Liu and Richmond, 2000); this suggests that rhinal cortex is doing more than a simple monosynaptic transformation of visual input from TE neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of longer-than-expected delays

claim: A variety of manipulations that increased the perceptual difficulty of a categorization task revealed significant, although far from catastrophic, deficits in monkeys with bilateral TE removals.
source: In the current study, a variety of manipulations that increased the perceptual difficulty of a categorization task revealed significant, although far from catastrophic, deficits in monkeys with bilateral TE removals, and no deficits in monkeys with bilateral rhinal removals.
evidence: Stated as a summary of the experimental findings

claim: A variety of manipulations that increased the perceptual difficulty of a categorization task revealed no deficits in monkeys with bilateral rhinal removals.
source: In the current study, a variety of manipulations that increased the perceptual difficulty of a categorization task revealed significant, although far from catastrophic, deficits in monkeys with bilateral TE removals, and no deficits in monkeys with bilateral rhinal removals.
evidence: Stated as a summary of the experimental findings

claim: The final stage of image processing in the ventral visual stream appears to occur in area TE.
source: Thus, the final stage of image processing in the ventral visual stream appears to occur in area TE.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the experimental results

claim: Rhinal cortex is critical for learning and remembering contextual or associative relations among stimuli or events.
source: Rhinal cortex is critical for learning and remembering contextual or associative relations among stimuli or events, but appears to play no role in object percept formation.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion integrating current and prior findings

claim: Rhinal cortex appears to play no role in object percept formation.
source: Rhinal cortex is critical for learning and remembering contextual or associative relations among stimuli or events, but appears to play no role in object percept formation.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the experimental results

claim: Three monkeys had previously received bilateral aspiration removals of area TE 2 years prior to the commencement of this study.
source: Three monkeys (5 – 6 years old, weighing 6.9 – 9.0 kg) had previously received bilateral aspiration removals of area TE 2 years prior to the commencement of this study; the reconstructions of these lesions have been published previously (Matsumoto et al., 2016).
